source: CSB Case Study 2013-03-I-LA: Sections 1.0, 4.0-4.1 (pp. 5, 14-15), 5.0 (pp. 22-39), Key Lessons (p. 56), Conclusions (p. 57), Recommendations R1-R5 (pp. 58-59), Appendix B failure scenario analysis (pp. 66-72). All withheld from the agent.
question: Failure mechanism, pressures, why unprotected, and prevention for the 2013 Williams Geismar reboiler rupture.

items.engineers: Liquid propane accumulated in the standby, isolated Reboiler B shell over the 16 months (leaking or mistakenly opened block valves; gate valves leak), at least about 65 vol% full; there was no instrumentation to detect process fluid in the standby reboiler.
leak_phrases: flammable liquid propane accumulated on the shell side of the standby Reboiler B

items.engineers: Introducing 187 F quench water heated the liquid-full, blocked-in propane: liquid thermal (hydraulic) expansion overpressured the shell (theoretically up to about 5,000 psig); metallurgy shows failure between 674 and 1,212 psig, above the 300 psig MAWP and 450 psig hydrotest, leading to a BLEVE and fire. The equilibrium vapour pressure at 187 F (about 496 psig) alone is not enough to explain the rupture.
leak_phrases: likely the result of liquid thermal expansion in the liquid propane-filled and blocked-in Reboiler B shell

items.engineers: The block valves added in 2001 isolated each reboiler from its only pressure relief valve on top of the propylene fractionator; the standby reboiler had no relief device of its own, so a closed shell-side valve left it unprotected.
leak_phrases: isolated from its protective pressure relief valve

items.engineers: Deficient MOC for the 2001 valve installation (hazard of isolating from relief not identified), poor PSSR, PHA action item (car-seal open the valves / add relief) not effectively implemented or verified, no adequate written procedure for switching reboilers, and the supervisor manipulated equipment without a procedure or hazard assessment.

Install a pressure relief device on each reboiler (new design adopted post-incident) rather than relying on car seals or administrative controls (hierarchy of controls); use positive isolation such as blinds for standby or out-of-service equipment.

Improve MOC, PSSR, PHA action item closure and operating procedures (including non-routine operations); process safety culture assessments and process safety metrics; API 521 should define standby/out-of-service equipment and require a relief device where hydraulic expansion can exceed the design code pressure.
